newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian chemicals industry needs reform -report.
newsitem.headline: Australian chemicals industry needs reform -report.

text.p: The Australian chemicals and plastics industry was in danger of stagnating if it did not substantially improve its competitiveness, an industry group warned on Tuesday.

Plastic and Chemicals Industries Association president John Foote said a study prepared by Access Economics had found Australia was not an attractive place for chemicals investment when compared to its Asian neighbours.
"The Australian chemical industry ... must be at least as good as anybody else in the world," Foote told reporters.
"Unless we are as good as or better than our competitors, the industry in Australia will simply not grow."
He said without drastic investment climate improvements, multinational chemical companies would continue to take their new projects elsewhere.
"The current situation is serious and we are letting ourselves down as other countries profit," he said.
The study found the major impediments to investment in the industry were:
-- the lack of competitive investment incentives;
-- the lack of an effective anti-dumping system;
-- the need to improve market access through the removal of tariff and non-tariff barriers in overseas markets; and
Foote said the study had prompted the industry to call on the government to develop a taskforce aimed at removing these impediments to investment.
He said he welcomed the government's move to reform the taxation system and the possible introduction of a goods and services tax (GST).
"I think a GST would be a step in the right direction along with a major reform of our total taxation policy," he said.
Tax reforms should include a reduction of taxes on inputs and the removal or lowering of taxes on exports, he said.
